conclusions: Both policies plotted at achieved sampled error, with observed min-max ranges.
Dense reduces RHS sharply for observation-limited simple cases; rapid reduction is small because oscillation resolution dominates.
Tight-target dense losses and noisy envelopes remain visible; three repetitions are not confidence intervals.

findings.observation: Random receipt order combined with seekable gzip archive access repeatedly decompresses archived data. Frozen analyzer completed correctly; this is postprocessing cost, not solver failure.
findings.action: Read archive once in stream order and retain only small per-record scores/hashes; compare resulting numeric summaries bytewise or valuewise before adoption. Existing evidence/audit_final_benchmark.py demonstrates one-pass auditing.

findings.observation: Eligibility checks timed count and successful replays but does not require the exact unique warmup/timed round-key set. The actual campaign has all288 unique correct keys, independently verified, so current results are unaffected.
findings.action: Add campaign-level strict coverage validation and negative tests for duplicate timed IDs, missing warmup, foreign config, nonzero completed exit; refuse affected configurations instead of silently selecting them.

claim_limits: Same error cap is not exactly equal attained error; landing can over-resolve simple problems because every output must be an accepted endpoint.
All saved times were checked; no uniform-time or requested-rtol certificate is inferred.
This is a benchmark of new-source landing versus new-source dense policy, not proof of speedup from removing one poison pass.
Physical norm correctness is supported by targeted contracts; this campaign does not benchmark a full33 physical client.
Large vectors remain repeated diagonal fixtures and logistic/rapid are known preregistered validation models, not new blind data.
